meta.title: Who really said "I'd rather have a free bottle in front of me than a prefrontal lobotomy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker — she died in 1967 and the credit first surfaces in 1989. Quote Investigator traces the wordplay to a 1965 philosophy book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'd rather have a free bottle in front of me than a prefrontal lobotomy'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dorothy Parker. The earliest documented version of the bottle/lobotomy joke is a 1965 book by an Oklahoma philosophy professor.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — earliest in print is Carlton W. Berenda, 1965
answer.authorDates: American philosopher of science · Professor of Philosophy, University of Oklahoma
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator’s earliest match for this wordplay is Carlton W. Berenda’s 1965 book World Visions and the Image of Man, where it appears in a three-way form rather than the sentence people quote today. Steve Allen later claimed he ad-libbed the joke on stage, and QI names Berenda and Allen as its two leading candidates without settling between them. The familiar “free bottle…prefrontal lobotomy” wording is not documented until 1977.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the line is real and old, but no one has established who wrote it, and Dorothy Parker is ruled out on dates alone.

source.heading: The earliest documented appearance

docMeta.dd: World Visions and the Image of Man: Cosmologies as Reflections of Man
Carlton W. Berenda, Professor of Philosophy, University of Oklahoma
New York: Vantage Press, 1965 — quote page 196
A three-way pun, not the modern one-liner

source.excerpt: And the male, confronted with this creature from day to day, may be driven to reflect upon three alternatives: “A bottle in front of me, a frontal lobotomy, or the front off the bottom of me!”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the wordplay to Carlton W. Berenda’s 1965 book World Visions and the Image of Man (New York: Vantage Press, quote page 196), where it runs “A bottle in front of me, a frontal lobotomy, or the front off the bottom of me!” — a three-way pun, not the sentence quoted today.

The familiar wording arrives twelve years later. QI’s earliest match for it is a pub graffito reported by San Francisco Chronicle columnist Herb Caen in March 1977, and Tom Waits used the joke on television that August — QI notes ↗ he “used the joke in 1977 after it was already in circulation.”

Steve Allen claimed coinage in his 1987 book How To Be Funny ↗, describing it as an accident on stage. QI records that the earliest published proof of Allen using the line is a November 1976 broadcast — eleven years after Berenda — and so names the two of them as “the two top candidates” rather than choosing.

Dorothy Parker died on 7 June 1967 ↗. The earliest credit to her that QI documents is a Fresno Bee column of 22 November 1989, and QI’s verdict is unambiguous: “The attributions to Dorothy Parker and Fred Allen are unsupported.”
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗, which records the page as verified visually by a librarian at the John C. Hodges Library. The Internet Archive’s copy of the book is lending-restricted, so we could not read page 196 ourselves.
source.rightsNote: The familiar “free bottle…prefrontal lobotomy” wording has no identifiable author — QI ↗ first documents it as an anonymous pub graffito in 1977, and names Berenda’s 1965 book and Steve Allen’s nightclub act as the two candidate origins of the underlying joke. Every candidate origin is well after 1930, so this is certainly not a public-domain text; but with no settled author there is no identifiable rights holder, so we assert no status.

author.name: Carlton W. Berenda
author.heading: About Carlton W. Berenda
author.metaLine: American philosopher of science · Professor of Philosophy, University of Oklahoma
author.bio: Carlton W. Berenda was an American philosopher of science who taught at the University of Oklahoma, and who is listed among the contributors to the 1967 Encyclopedia of Philosophy. His 1965 book World Visions and the Image of Man argued that competing cosmologies reflect the self-image of the people who hold them. He is remembered by quotation researchers for a single parenthetical joke on page 196 — almost certainly not the thing he hoped the book would be known for.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most redistributed “Dorothy Parker” lines online. It is not hers — and it is not clearly anyone’s.

items.why: Parker died in June 1967. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no attribution to her until a Fresno Bee column of 22 November 1989 — twenty-two years after her death — and concludes that the attributions to Parker “are unsupported.”

Allen claimed in his 1987 book How To Be Funny ↗ that he invented the line by accident on stage. QI accepts him as a leading candidate but notes his earliest published use is November 1976, eleven years after Berenda’s book.
Waits used the joke on the television show Fernwood 2 Night in August 1977. QI ↗ states plainly that he “used the joke in 1977 after it was already in circulation.”
A November 1989 Kentucky newspaper column tentatively credited the line to Prine as a song title. QI ↗ answers flatly: “Prine did not sing the tune, and it may not even be a song.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented instance belongs to a University of Oklahoma philosophy professor, buried in a 1965 book about cosmology — and even he may have picked it up from a nightclub stage. Read QI’s full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it drifted
lead: A pun this clean has no natural owner, so it attaches itself to whoever the audience already thinks is funny. Between 1977 and 1989 the same sentence was credited in print to a graffiti artist, Tom Waits, Steve Allen, John Prine and Dorothy Parker — and it survived every reassignment intact, because nobody was checking.

Parker is the strongest magnet of the five. She really did produce a lifetime of compressed, cruel one-liners, so a compressed cruel one-liner sounds like her by default — which is exactly the reasoning that fails, and exactly why Wikiquote’s Parker page opens with a standing warning about the volume of misquotation attached to her name.
context.pull: The joke outlived every author it was assigned.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI names Berenda's 1965 book World Visions and the Image of Man (Vantage Press, quote page 196) as the earliest match, and reproduces the wording "A bottle in front of me, a frontal lobotomy, or the front off the bottom of me!"
QI concludes "The attributions to Dorothy Parker and Fred Allen are unsupported" and records the earliest Parker credit as the Fresno Bee, 22 November 1989.
QI states Tom Waits "used the joke in 1977 after it was already in circulation", and that Steve Allen claimed coinage in his 1987 book while his earliest published use is November 1976.
Berenda's World Visions and the Image of Man (1965) is a real book, catalogued by the Internet Archive under that author and year. The scan is lending-restricted, so its text was not read here.
Steve Allen's How to Be Funny: Discovering the Comic You (1987) is catalogued by the Internet Archive.
Robert Byrne's The 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (1982) is catalogued by the Internet Archive.

Wikiquote gives Dorothy Parker's dates as 22 August 1893 to 7 June 1967 and opens its page with a warning that many misquotations are attributed to her; its Misattributed section does NOT list the bottle/lobotomy line.
Steve Allen (1921-2000) was an American comedian, musician and television host.
